```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(bayesrules)
library(ggformula)
library(broom)
library(patchwork)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
source("notes-helpers.R")

bikes <- bikes |> select(date, season, year, month, weekend, holiday,
                          temp_actual, temp_feel, humidity, windspeed, rides)

bikes_A <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend, data = bikes)
bikes_B <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend + holiday, data = bikes)
bikes_C <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend + holiday + humidity, data = bikes)
bikes_D <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual + windspeed + weekend + holiday + humidity + temp_feel, data = bikes)
bikes_E <- lm(rides ~ temp_feel + humidity + weekend + holiday, data = bikes)
n_bikes <- nrow(bikes)
```

## Review: sums of squares

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 2.6
x <- c(1, 2.5, 4, 6, 8, 9.5)
y <- c(1.5, 4, 3.5, 7, 7.5, 10)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
df$y_hat <- predict(fit)
df$y_mean <- mean(df$y)

make_squares <- function(data, y1_col, y2_col, color) {
  data$diff <- data[[y1_col]] - data[[y2_col]]
  geom_rect(data = data, aes(
    xmin = x,
    xmax = x + abs(diff),
    ymin = pmin(data[[y1_col]], data[[y2_col]]),
    ymax = pmax(data[[y1_col]], data[[y2_col]])
  ), fill = color, alpha = 0.3, color = color)
}

p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = y_mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  make_squares(df, "y", "y_mean", "blue") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "SST") +
  coord_fixed()

p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = y_mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_hat), color = "darkgreen") +
  make_squares(df, "y_hat", "y_mean", "darkgreen") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "SSReg") +
  coord_fixed()

p3 <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_hat), color = "darkgreen") +
  make_squares(df, "y", "y_hat", "red") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "SSE") +
  coord_fixed()

p1 | p2 | p3
```

-   Least squares makes the total area of the ______________ squares
    as small as possible
-   $R^2$: proportion of the ______________ area (SST) covered by the
    ______________ squares (SSReg)
-   $R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{MSE}{MST}$: same idea, but each model is
    "charged" for the number of ______________ it uses
-   Overall $F$ test, $F = \frac{MSReg}{MSE}$: is the "average"
    ______________ square bigger than the "average" ______________ square?
-   Extra sums of squares $F$ test: are the ______________ squares for a
    larger model significantly smaller than for a smaller model?

## Today: building an *explanatory* model

**Question:** How are weekends and holidays associated with ridership,
after accounting for the weather?

Two reasons to build a model:

-   **Explanatory:** ___________________________________________________
-   **Predictive:** ___________________________________________________

Today we're building an explanatory model. (Predictive models come after
the quiz!)

## A recipe for explanatory models

1.  **Start with the question.** Which variables are you interested in?
    Which do you need to adjust for? These stay in the model, even if
    ___________________________
2.  **Look before you fit.** Check for predictors that
    ___________________________
3.  **Fit a *small* set of candidate models** (not every possible
    combination!)
4.  **Compare the candidates**: ______________ for nested models;
    ______________ for any models
5.  **Check the conditions** for the model you choose
6.  **Interpret and justify** your choice

## Step 1: Our candidate models

-   **Interested in:** `weekend`, `holiday`
-   **Adjust for:** weather (temperature, windspeed, humidity)

| Model | Predictors |
|:--|:--|

| B | A + `holiday` |
| C | B + `humidity` |
| D | C + `temp_feel` |

## Step 3: Compare nested models with an $F$ test

Two models are **nested** if the reduced model is a ____________________ of the
full model (we get it by setting some $\beta$'s equal to ______).

**Which pairs are nested?** Circle one for each.

| Model 1 | Model 2 | Nested? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | B | yes / no |
| B | D | yes / no |
| C | E | yes / no |
| A | C | yes / no |

$$F = \frac{(SSE_{reduced} - SSE_{full}) / d}{SSE_{full} / df_{full}}$$

-   Numerator: ______________________________________________
-   Denominator: ______________________________________________
-   A large $F$ means: ______________________________________________

**Adding variables one at a time:**

```{r}
step_tab <- bind_rows(
  tidy(anova(bikes_A, bikes_B)) |> slice(2) |> mutate(step = "A to B: add holiday"),
  tidy(anova(bikes_B, bikes_C)) |> slice(2) |> mutate(step = "B to C: add humidity"),
  tidy(anova(bikes_C, bikes_D)) |> slice(2) |> mutate(step = "C to D: add temp_feel")
) |>
  select(step, d = df, F = statistic, `p-value` = p.value) |>
  mutate(`p-value` = fmt_p(`p-value`))
knitr::kable(step_tab, digits = 2)
```

What do the $F$ tests say about each step?

\vspace{.75in}

## Careful: `temp_actual` and `temp_feel`

```{r}
bind_rows(
  tidy(bikes_C) |> filter(term == "temp_actual") |> mutate(model = "C (without temp_feel)"),
  tidy(bikes_D) |> filter(term %in% c("temp_actual", "temp_feel")) |> mutate(model = "D (with temp_feel)")
) |>
  select(model, term, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  mutate(p.value = fmt_p(p.value)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

What happened to the standard error of `temp_actual`? Why? What should we
do?

\vspace{.75in}

We need tools that work for *any* two models fit to the same data.

## Adjusted $R^2$

$$R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{MSE}{MST} = 1 - \frac{SSE/(n-(p+1))}{SST/(n-1)}$$

-   $R^2$ always goes up when we add predictors; $R^2_{adj}$ ______________
-   can be used for nested **and** non-nested models
-   no formal test or rule for "better enough"

```{r}
tibble(Model = c("C: temp_actual + windspeed + weekend + holiday + humidity",
                 "E: temp_feel + humidity + weekend + holiday"),
       `Adj R2` = c(summary(bikes_C)$adj.r.squared, summary(bikes_E)$adj.r.squared)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Which model does adjusted $R^2$ prefer? ________________

## Information criteria: AIC and BIC

$$IC = \text{Measure of Fit} + \text{Penalty}$$

$$AIC = n \log(SSE/n) + 2k \qquad\qquad BIC = n \log(SSE/n) + \log(n) \cdot k$$

where $k$ = number of coefficients (**including** the intercept). In R:
`AIC(model)` and `BIC(model)`.

-   Smaller values are ______________.
-   When we add a predictor, the fit term gets ______________ and the penalty gets ______________.
-   BIC penalizes more than AIC whenever $\log(n) >$ ______, i.e. $n \ge$ ______.

## Example: adjusted $R^2$ and $F$ tests by hand

A researcher fits four nested models to $n = 40$ observations. Fill in the
table, then answer the questions.

| Model | Predictors | $p$ | SSE | $\hat\sigma^2 = SSE/(n-(p+1))$ | $R^2_{adj}$ |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| M0 | none | 0 | 980 | | |
| M1 | $x_1$ | 1 | 520 | | |
| M2 | $x_1, x_2$ | 2 | 410 | | |
| M3 | $x_1, x_2, x_3$ | 3 | 398 | | |

$R^2_{adj} = 1 - \hat\sigma^2 / \hat\sigma^2_{M0}$ (since $MST = SSE_{M0}/(n-1)$).

\vspace{2in}

**(a)** Which model is best by $R^2_{adj}$?

\vspace{.5in}

**(b)** Use an $F$ test to compare M2 to M1 and M3 to M2. State $d$ and $df_{full}$ each time.

\vspace{1.5in}

**(c)** Do the two tools agree? Which model would you choose?

## Comparing two models

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 5
graph TD
    classDef default fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px,color:#1b5e20;

    A(["Are the models nested?"])
    B(["Do they differ by<br>one coefficient?"])
    C["t-test for that coefficient<br>(same as the F test)"]
    D["Extra sums of squares F test<br>anova(reduced, full)"]
    E["Adjusted R², AIC, or BIC<br>(no p-value)"]
    F["If the tools disagree,<br>choose the simpler model"]

    A -->|YES| B
    A -->|NO| E
    B -->|YES| C
    B -->|NO| D
    C --> F
    D --> F
    E --> F
```

## Summary

| Tool | Nested only? | Gives a p-value? | Notes |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| $F$ test | | | |
| Adjusted $R^2$ | | | |
| AIC | | | |
| BIC | | | |

-   Use domain knowledge first. These tools compare candidate models; they
    don't replace thinking.
-   **Justify your model choice!**
